title: Petition calls for Canadian telcos to answer customer calls within 10 minutes
summary: An Ontario man says Canadians are fed up with long waits for telecom customer service. He’s launched a petition urging the federal government to require telcos to connect customers with a human agent…

image.caption: Frank Brown and hundreds of other Canadians have signed a petition he started, calling on the government to make companies like Rogers, Bell and Telus answer the phone — with a human agent — within 10 minutes. (Craig Chivers/CBC)

blocks.text: Frank Brown spent almost an hour on hold with Rogers last June, while simultaneously trying to get help through the company's online chat.
The Aurora, Ont., man was trying to find out why a $25 charge had appeared on his mother's account, which he manages.
After more than 40 minutes, he says he gave up on the chat because it wasn't helping. He soon abandoned the call, too.
Two days later, he tried calling Rogers again. This time he couldn't even get into the queue. A recorded message told him the system was overloaded and too busy to take his call.
"It isn't customer service if you can't talk to anybody," Brown said.
"Access to a human representative should not be treated as an additional premium service."

blocks.text: For the last few months, Brown's been on a mission to get the federal government to take the issue seriously, launching a petition urging Ottawa to force telecom providers to connect with a human agent within 10 minutes.
"There is no measurable customer service standard in this industry," said Brown. "We need to make sure consumers are protected."
This man started a petition to force telcos to answer customer calls within 10 minutes | Go Public
Brown isn't alone in his frustration.
Long wait times, dropped calls, unhelpful agents and automated systems have sent customers in circles — frustrations Go Public and CBC Marketplace have documented across the country.

items: Customers complain about long wait times, multiple calls to resolve issues with Rogers, Telus and Bell
Telecom complaints have shot up 17%, with billing issues the main gripe, says watchdog

blocks.text: Complaints to the Commission for Complaints for Telecom-television Services (CCTS) were up 79 per cent in 2025-2026 over the previous year — ranging from billing and contract disputes to cancellation issues — but the telecom mediator has no mandate to specifically address customer service complaints, such as long wait times. That leaves customers with no independent avenue to complain about the very service they're struggling to access.
And customer service has deteriorated dramatically, according to Mohammed Halabi, whose company MyBillsAreHigh.com helps businesses and individuals save money on telecom and internet costs.
"They've got to be held to account somehow," Halabi said. "The government has to do something."
Mohammed Halabi helps telco customers lower their bills. He says customer service has become 'absolutely horrible' over the last two years. (Michael Cole/CBC)
Go Public asked Rogers, Bell and Telus how they respond to calls for a mandatory 10-minute standard for answering customer calls.

Rogers declined an interview. A spokesperson sent a written statement saying the average wait time to reach a customer service representative was "around 7 minutes" this year — that figure does not include people on hold who give up after not getting through, like Brown. Rogers said a "very small percentage" of callers hang up before reaching a customer service rep and that the company is continuing to improve "the customer experience."
Telus and Bell both wrote that the "vast majority" of customer calls are answered within minutes.
Neither would specify what percentage of callers hang up after failing to reach a human agent — like Rogers, those customers are not included in their wait-time averages.
A growing chorus of complaints

After Brown filed a complaint with the CCTS, Rogers credited the $25 charge to his mother's account in July, calling it a "goodwill gesture." The company told Go Public it understood Brown had a "frustrating experience."

Since then, he's had to make several more calls to his telecom provider about other issues. Rogers says on average, Brown spent about four minutes getting routed to a customer service rep — but he says his concerns stand.
He initially launched a petition on Change.org, a petition platform, asking Canadians to support his call for better response times. So far, over 1,200 have signed.
Some have left comments describing two-hour waits, calling the delays "disgusting" and saying they felt "held hostage" on the phone.
Frank Brown spent nearly an hour on hold trying to resolve an issue with his mother's bill. (Submitted by Frank Brown)
Go Public has also received plenty of complaints from customers. Most emails are about Rogers, but some customers have also described difficulties getting through to Bell and Telus.
"It should not be this hard [to close an account]," wrote one person. "What in the world is going on with this company?"
"We have documented 18 separate call attempts totalling over 10.5 hours attempting to resolve this issue," wrote another.
"They keep laying people off, but cannot answer their phone," wrote another.
Customer service 'absolutely horrible'
Halabi says telecom customer service has become "absolutely horrible" over the last two years.

During that time, all three major telcos have laid off or offered buyouts to segments of their Canadian workforces. According to Unifor telecommunications director Roch LeBlanc, roughly 20,000 telecommunications jobs have been lost due to automation and offshoring in the last 10 to 15 years.
"It's just gotten so bad," Halabi said. "It's a constant circus."

blocks.text: He also believes telecom companies are increasingly trying to push artificial intelligence over the use of human agents — technology that can frustrate customers when it misunderstands what callers are saying or directs them to the wrong department.
"All of this is creating a sense of anxiety, especially for senior citizens."
Spain's new 3-minute law

Before retiring two years ago, Brown spent eight years as president of a company that employed dozens of people. For years, he says, he personally responded to every consumer review because he wanted customers to know "the person at the top" cared about their business.

"I hate the hypocrisy of Rogers courting me on TV — as if me giving them my business is very much appreciated — and then hearing ‘your call is important to us' while waiting forever for them to answer the phone," he told Go Public.
Brown believes telecom companies should be held to a measurable customer-service standard, as is the case in Spain.

Spain passed legislation last December requiring companies with more than 250 employees to ensure that when customers request a human agent, they can reach one within three minutes in 95 per cent of cases.
"Three minutes is pretty aggressive," said Brown, which is why he thought a 10-minute standard would be a reasonable starting point here.
"It's the Canadian way, we're nice people."
Telecom complaints soar as Canadians rail over billing issues

Hoping to get action from the federal government, Brown also launched a parliamentary petition, which would compel a written response from the government should it reach 500 signatures by Nov. 26. As of Nov. 19, it was sitting at 425 signatures.

The petition calls on the federal government to direct the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) to establish "clear, measurable and enforceable" customer service standards for telecommunications providers.

Specifically, it calls for a "maximum 10-minute telephone hold time" for customers seeking access to a human agent and requests "meaningful and proportional consequences" for providers that persistently fail to meet that standard.
"There is no measurable customer service standard in this industry," said Brown. "As long as we're going to limit competition in the industry, we need to make sure that us consumers are protected."

blocks.text: Brown is also scheduled to discuss his petitions when he appears before the CRTC next week, as it begins hearings on protections for home phone, wireless, TV and internet consumers.
"There's a real feeling that we just have to accept [bad customer service]," he said. "And I decided, no, I'm going to try and do something about it."
